questions.stem: A 67 year old man has been using wooden axillary crutches for 3 weeks after a tibial fracture, leaning heavily on them. He now cannot straighten his right elbow against resistance or extend his right wrist and fingers. The triceps reflex is absent and there is numbness over the back of the arm and hand.
questions.q: Which is the most likely site of the nerve lesion?
o: Posterior interosseous nerve at the elbow
Radial nerve at the spiral groove
questions.e: Crutch pressure in the axilla injures the radial nerve high up, so triceps as well as the wrist and finger extensors are weak.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely site of the nerve lesion?
Weak elbow extension plus wrist drop means a lesion above the triceps branches, which is the axilla.

elim: Median nerve lesions at the wrist cause thenar weakness and lateral finger numbness, not loss of extension.
This low radial lesion causes finger drop with intact triceps and sensation.
A spiral groove lesion causes wrist drop but spares triceps, because its branches leave above the groove.
Ulnar lesions weaken intrinsic hand muscles and cause medial hand numbness.

steps.x: Answer D: Radial nerve in the axilla. Wrist drop + weak triceps = high (axillary) radial nerve lesion, e.g. crutch palsy.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman fractured her left radial head falling off a bicycle 2 weeks ago. She can extend her wrist but cannot extend her fingers at the metacarpophalangeal joints. When she extends her wrist it deviates radially. Sensation in the hand is normal and the triceps reflex is present.
questions.q: Which is the most likely nerve lesion?
o: High radial nerve lesion in the axilla
Low radial nerve lesion (posterior interosseous nerve) at the elbow
Median nerve injury at the elbow
Radial nerve lesion at the spiral groove
Ulnar nerve injury at the elbow
questions.e: A low radial nerve injury at the elbow (radial head fracture) causes finger drop with intact sensation, as the superficial sensory branch is spared.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely nerve lesion?

clues: Sensation in the hand is normal
steps.x: Finger drop without wrist drop or sensory loss localises to the forearm level of the radial nerve.

elim: An axillary lesion would weaken triceps and cause sensory loss.
Median lesions weaken finger flexion, not extension.
A spiral groove lesion causes wrist drop with sensory loss over the first web space.
Ulnar injury causes clawing and weak finger abduction, not finger drop.

steps.x: Answer B: Low radial nerve lesion (posterior interosseous nerve) at the elbow. Radial head fracture: finger drop with intact sensation (low radial / posterior interosseous lesion).

questions.stem: A 61 year old man has 4 months of numbness of his left little finger and the medial edge of his hand. He leans on his elbows at work all day. There is wasting of the first dorsal interosseous and his ring and little fingers are clawed. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which additional finding on examination is most likely if the lesion is at the elbow?
o: Radial deviation of the wrist on resisted wrist flexion
questions.e: At the elbow the ulnar nerve supplies flexor carpi ulnaris, so wrist flexion pulls radially; there is also weak finger abduction/adduction and medial hand sensory loss.

steps.x: The question asks: Which additional finding on examination is most likely if the lesion is at the elbow?

clues: ring and little fingers are clawed
numbness of his left little finger
steps.x: Clawing of the 4th/5th fingers is ulnar; an elbow lesion also loses FCU.

elim: The biceps reflex is C5/C6, not ulnar nerve.
Phalen's test is positive in carpal tunnel syndrome (median nerve).
Thenar wasting is a median nerve sign.
Wrist drop is a radial nerve sign.

steps.x: Answer C: Radial deviation of the wrist on resisted wrist flexion. Ulnar lesion at the elbow loses FCU: radial deviation on wrist flexion.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has 8 months of tingling in her right thumb, index and middle fingers that wakes her at night and is eased by shaking her hand. Tinel's test at the wrist reproduces her tingling. She now drops cups. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on inspection of her hand?
o: Clawing of the ring and little fingers
Swan neck deformity of the little finger only
questions.e: Carpal tunnel syndrome causes thenar (not hypothenar) wasting and weak thumb abduction (abductor pollicis brevis).

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on inspection of her hand?

clues: thumb, index and middle fingers that wakes her at night
steps.x: Median nerve compression at the wrist, associated with RA, weakens and wastes the thenar muscles.

elim: Clawing of the 4th/5th fingers is an ulnar nerve sign.
This is a rheumatoid joint deformity and does not explain her nerve symptoms.
The hypothenar muscles are ulnar supplied and are spared in carpal tunnel syndrome.
Wrist drop is a radial nerve sign.

steps.x: Answer D: Wasting of the thenar eminence. Carpal tunnel: thenar wasting, weak APB; hypothenar spared.

questions.stem: A 28 year old man was kicked hard on the front of his right upper shin playing football 3 weeks ago. He now drags his right toes when walking. He cannot dorsiflex his right ankle, but eversion is normal and ankle and knee reflexes are present. He has numbness only between his first and second toes.
questions.q: Which nerve is most likely injured?
questions.e: The deep peroneal branch causes foot drop with sensory loss in the first web space, with eversion and reflexes preserved.

steps.x: The question asks: Which nerve is most likely injured?

clues: cannot dorsiflex his right ankle, but eversion is normal
numbness only between his first and second toes
steps.x: Isolated foot drop with first web space numbness and normal eversion localises to the deep branch.

elim: A common peroneal lesion would also weaken eversion and cause wider sensory loss over the lateral leg.
An L5 root lesion would also weaken inversion and hip abduction, with sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot.
The sural nerve is sensory to the lateral foot and does not cause foot drop.
Tibial lesions weaken plantar flexion and inversion, with sole numbness.

steps.x: Answer B: Deep peroneal nerve. Foot drop + first web space numbness + normal eversion = deep peroneal nerve.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man has a left foot drop. His GP is unsure whether it is a common peroneal nerve palsy after he spent a long time kneeling while tiling, or an L5 radiculopathy from his long-standing back pain. Ankle dorsiflexion and eversion are weak. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which finding on examination would most support a common peroneal nerve palsy?
o: Pain radiating down the posterior thigh
Sensory loss over the sole of the foot
questions.e: Common peroneal palsy causes isolated loss of dorsiflexion and eversion; loss of inversion as well suggests an L5 root lesion.

steps.x: The question asks: Which finding on examination would most support a common peroneal nerve palsy?

clues: Ankle dorsiflexion and eversion are weak
steps.x: Inversion is tibialis posterior (tibial nerve, L5), so it is spared in peroneal palsy but weak in L5 lesions.

elim: An absent ankle reflex points to an S1 root lesion, not a peroneal palsy.
Neuropathic pain down the posterior thigh is a feature of L5 radiculopathy.
The sole is supplied by the tibial nerve.
Weak hip abduction is an L5 root sign, as gluteus medius is supplied by L5 via the superior gluteal nerve.

steps.x: Answer B: Normal strength of ankle inversion. Preserved inversion = common peroneal palsy; weak inversion + eversion = L5.

questions.stem: A 3 day old girl was delivered by breech extraction with forceful traction on her arm above her head. Her right hand lies limp with clawed fingers and she does not grip. The right upper eyelid droops and the right pupil is smaller than the left. Shoulder and elbow movements are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Klumpke's palsy (lower plexus, C8/T1) paralyses the small hand muscles with dermatomal sensory disturbance and possible Horner's syndrome (ptosis).

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: traction on her arm above her head
steps.x: Arm pulled above the head stretches the lower roots; T1 damage also interrupts sympathetic fibres.

elim: Erb's (C5/C6) affects the shoulder and elbow, giving the waiter's tip posture with a normal hand.
A fractured clavicle causes pain and reduced arm movement without hand clawing or Horner's.
A median palsy does not cause ptosis or miosis.
Radial palsy causes wrist drop, not clawing and Horner's.

steps.x: Answer C: Klumpke's palsy. Klumpke's = C8/T1: small hand muscle paralysis ± Horner's.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman had a left mastectomy with axillary node clearance 3 weeks ago. She now has pain around her left shoulder and difficulty lifting her arm forwards above her head. When she pushes against a wall, the medial border of her left scapula lifts away from the chest wall.
questions.q: Which nerve is most likely injured?
questions.e: Long thoracic nerve injury paralyses serratus anterior, causing scapular winging with shoulder girdle pain and instability on flexion/abduction.

steps.x: The question asks: Which nerve is most likely injured?

clues: medial border of her left scapula lifts away
steps.x: Winging on wall push = serratus anterior weakness; its nerve runs on the chest wall in the axilla.

elim: Axillary nerve injury weakens deltoid and causes lateral shoulder numbness, not winging.
This weakens elbow flexion and causes lateral forearm numbness.
Radial injury causes wrist drop.
This weakens initiation of abduction and external rotation, without winging.

steps.x: Answer B: Long thoracic nerve. Scapular winging = long thoracic nerve.

questions.stem: A 23 year old rugby player had an anterior dislocation of his right shoulder reduced in the emergency department. Afterwards he cannot raise his arm sideways and has a numb patch on the outer upper arm over the lower part of the deltoid. Radial pulse is present. His pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which nerve is most likely injured?
questions.e: The axillary nerve is injured in shoulder dislocation and surgical neck fractures; test sensation over the lower lateral deltoid.

steps.x: The question asks: Which nerve is most likely injured?

clues: anterior dislocation of his right shoulder
numb patch on the outer upper arm over the lower part of the deltoid
steps.x: Deltoid weakness plus a numb regimental badge area = axillary nerve.

elim: Long thoracic injury causes scapular winging.
Median injury affects finger flexion and lateral hand sensation.
Radial injury causes wrist drop and dorsal hand numbness.
Ulnar injury causes clawing and medial hand numbness.

steps.x: Answer A: Axillary nerve. Shoulder dislocation + lateral deltoid numbness = axillary nerve.

questions.stem: A 52 year old decorator has 2 months of pain over the back of his right shoulder. He cannot start to lift his arm away from his side, although he can continue the movement if it is helped through the first part. With arms abducted, thumbs pointing down, he cannot resist downward pressure on the right. There is wasting above the spine of the scapula.
questions.q: Which nerve is most likely injured?
questions.e: Suprascapular nerve injury weakens supraspinatus: failure to initiate abduction and a weak Jobe's (empty can) test.

steps.x: The question asks: Which nerve is most likely injured?

clues: cannot start to lift his arm away from his side
wasting above the spine of the scapula
steps.x: Failure to initiate abduction and a positive empty can test mean supraspinatus, supplied by the suprascapular nerve.

elim: The axillary nerve supplies deltoid, which continues abduction after it is initiated.
This causes scapular winging.
This weakens elbow flexion.
This supplies latissimus dorsi, weakening adduction and extension.

steps.x: Answer D: Suprascapular nerve. Cannot initiate abduction + weak Jobe's test = suprascapular nerve.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes has had double vision for 2 days. His right eyelid droops and the right eye rests down and out. Both pupils are 3 mm and react normally to light. He has mild ache around the eye. His BP is 148/88 mmHg and HbA1c is 82 mmol/mol.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Diabetes causes a pupil-sparing medical third nerve palsy; a dilated pupil suggests a surgical cause such as a posterior communicating artery aneurysm.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause?
Down and out with ptosis is a third nerve palsy; a normal pupil makes a compressive lesion unlikely.

elim: Myasthenia causes fatigable ptosis and diplopia but not a fixed down and out eye.
An aneurysm compresses the outer pupillomotor fibres, so the pupil is dilated.
A sixth nerve palsy causes failure of abduction without ptosis.
Thyroid eye disease causes proptosis and restricted movement, not a third nerve pattern.

steps.x: Answer A: Diabetic (microvascular) third nerve palsy. Pupil-sparing third nerve palsy = diabetes; dilated pupil = PComm aneurysm.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman has gained 18 kg over the past year. She has 6 weeks of burning pain and numbness over the outer front of her right thigh, worse on standing and wearing a tight belt. Power, reflexes and straight leg raise are normal. Her BMI is 36 kg/m².
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Meralgia paraesthetica is compression of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh, giving burning lateral thigh pain; sudden weight gain is the key risk factor.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: burning pain and numbness over the outer front of her right thigh
Power, reflexes and straight leg raise are normal
steps.x: Purely sensory symptoms over the lateral thigh with normal power and reflexes, after weight gain.

elim: This causes foot drop and lateral leg numbness, not thigh pain.
Femoral palsy weakens knee extension and reduces the knee reflex.
L3 root lesions cause weakness and a reduced knee jerk, often with back pain.
This causes lateral hip tenderness, not burning numbness of the thigh.

steps.x: Answer D: Meralgia paraesthetica. Burning lateral thigh + weight gain + normal motor = meralgia paraesthetica.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man has 6 days of tingling in his feet and weakness that started in his legs and has spread to his arms. He had a sore throat 3 weeks ago. Both sides of his face are weak and all reflexes are absent. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 132/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Classic Guillain-Barré starts distally and ascends, with areflexia and sometimes facial diplegia, after an infection.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: started in his legs and has spread to his arms
Both sides of his face are weak
steps.x: Ascending weakness, areflexia and facial diplegia after an infection.

elim: This is a slowly progressive hereditary neuropathy over years, not days.
Miller Fisher starts proximally with the eyes: ataxia, areflexia and ophthalmoplegia.
Myasthenia causes fatigable weakness with preserved reflexes.
Cord lesions cause a sensory level and later upper motor neuron signs, not facial diplegia.

steps.x: Answer B: Guillain-Barré syndrome. Distal ascending weakness + areflexia post-infection = GBS.

questions.stem: A 19 year old woman has had difficulty running and frequent ankle sprains since her early teens. She has high-arched feet, thin lower legs below the knee, bilateral foot drop and reduced sensation in both feet. Ankle reflexes are absent. Her mother walks with a similar gait.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Charcot-Marie-Tooth, the most common hereditary peripheral neuropathy, is autosomal dominant with distal weakness, foot drop and reduced sensation.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: Her mother walks with a similar gait
steps.x: Slowly progressive distal neuropathy from childhood with an affected parent.

elim: This would not explain pes cavus, distal wasting from childhood and a family history.
Duchenne is X-linked, affects boys and causes proximal weakness.
Friedreich's is autosomal recessive with prominent ataxia and cardiomyopathy.
GBS is acute, developing over days to weeks.

steps.x: Answer B: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease. Hereditary distal neuropathy with foot drop and pes cavus = Charcot-Marie-Tooth.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man who smokes has 3 months of pain along the inner forearm and weakness when spreading his fingers apart. There is numbness along the ulnar edge of his forearm. His right pupil is small. His pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 140/86 mmHg.
questions.q: Which nerve root is most likely affected?
questions.e: A T1 lesion causes finger abduction weakness with pain and sensory loss along the ulnar forearm; in a smoker with Horner's think of an apical lung tumour.

steps.x: The question asks: Which nerve root is most likely affected?

clues: weakness when spreading his fingers apart
steps.x: Finger abduction is T1 (the interossei), with medial forearm sensory loss.

elim: C5 weakens deltoid and the supraspinatus/infraspinatus, with lateral upper arm numbness.
C6 causes pain to the thumb and index finger and a depressed brachioradialis reflex.
C7 weakens triceps with a depressed triceps reflex.
L1 supplies the groin, not the upper limb.

steps.x: Answer E: T1. Finger abduction weakness = T1.

questions.stem: A newborn boy weighing 4.6 kg was delivered after shoulder dystocia. His left arm hangs by his side, adducted and internally rotated, with the elbow extended and the wrist flexed. He grips normally with the left hand. The Moro reflex is absent on the left.
questions.q: Which nerve roots are most likely injured?
questions.e: Erb's palsy (C5/C6) from shoulder dystocia gives the waiter's tip: extended forearm, flexed wrist, internally rotated adducted arm.

steps.x: The question asks: Which nerve roots are most likely injured?
Waiter's tip posture with a normal grip means upper plexus roots.

elim: An isolated C7 injury does not produce this posture.
Lower roots give Klumpke's palsy, with small hand muscle paralysis and a weak grip.
These are lumbar roots supplying the leg.
These are thoracic roots that supply the chest wall.

steps.x: Answer A: C5 and C6. Erb's palsy = C5/C6, waiter's tip.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman fell from a horse and has a displaced fracture of the middle of her right humeral shaft. She cannot extend her right wrist or fingers. Elbow extension is normal. There is numbness over the back of her hand at the base of the thumb. The radial pulse is present.
questions.q: Which nerve is most likely injured?
o: Radial nerve at the spiral groove
questions.e: The radial nerve is most commonly injured at mid-humeral shaft fractures; a humeral-level lesion causes wrist drop with dorsal first web space numbness, sparing triceps.

steps.x: The question asks: Which nerve is most likely injured?

clues: middle of her right humeral shaft
steps.x: Wrist drop with normal triceps after a mid-shaft fracture localises to the spiral groove.

elim: The axillary nerve is injured at the surgical neck or in dislocation, weakening deltoid.
Median injury weakens finger flexion and causes lateral palmar numbness.
This causes finger drop with normal sensation and preserved wrist extension.
Ulnar injury causes clawing and medial hand numbness.

steps.x: Answer D: Radial nerve at the spiral groove. Mid-humeral fracture + wrist drop = radial nerve at the spiral groove.

questions.stem: A 7 year old boy has a displaced supracondylar fracture of the left humerus. After reduction he cannot bend the tip of his thumb or index finger to make an 'OK' sign and has reduced sensation over the palmar surface of the thumb, index and middle fingers. Capillary refill is 2 seconds and the radial pulse is present.
questions.q: Which nerve is most likely injured?
questions.e: Median nerve injury causes weak finger flexion and reduced sensation in the median distribution (lateral palm and fingers).

steps.x: The question asks: Which nerve is most likely injured?

clues: cannot bend the tip of his thumb or index finger
palmar surface of the thumb, index and middle fingers
steps.x: Weak finger flexion with lateral palmar numbness is a median nerve deficit.

elim: The axillary nerve supplies deltoid and is not injured at the elbow.
This causes weak elbow flexion and lateral forearm numbness.
Radial injury causes weak wrist and finger extension.
Ulnar injury causes clawing of the 4th/5th fingers and medial hand numbness.

steps.x: Answer B: Median nerve. Weak finger flexion + lateral palmar numbness = median nerve.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man has 5 months of numbness of his right little finger and weakness of his hand grip. He has neck pain and also leans on his elbows at work. Examination shows weak finger abduction and reduced sensation over the medial hand, but it is unclear whether the lesion is at the C8 root or the ulnar nerve at the elbow.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to localise the lesion?
questions.e: Clinical examination is the gold standard, but nerve conduction studies and EMG are used when needed to localise or confirm the lesion.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation to localise the lesion?

clues: unclear whether the lesion is at the C8 root or the ulnar nerve
steps.x: Examination cannot separate root from nerve here, so electrophysiology is needed.

elim: The brain is not the suspected site.
X-ray shows bone, not nerve function.
CK reflects muscle damage and does not localise a nerve lesion.
The median nerve at the wrist is not the suspected lesion.

steps.x: Answer B: Nerve conduction studies and electromyography. NCS/EMG localise a peripheral nerve lesion when examination is unclear.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman sustained a fracture of the left fibular head in a skiing accident a week ago. She has a high-stepping gait, cannot dorsiflex or evert her left foot and has numbness over the outer leg and top of the foot. Inversion and reflexes are normal. Pulses are present.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate way to make the diagnosis?
questions.e: Clinical examination is the gold standard for diagnosing a peripheral nerve injury; this common fibular palsy after a fibular head fracture is clear clinically.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate way to make the diagnosis?

clues: fracture of the left fibular head
steps.x: The pattern is classic for common fibular palsy; no test is needed to make the diagnosis.

elim: CT shows the fracture, not the nerve deficit, which is already clear clinically.
CSF analysis is for GBS or infection, not a focal nerve injury.
Preserved inversion makes an L5 root lesion unlikely.
B12 deficiency causes a symmetrical neuropathy, not a focal palsy after a fracture.

steps.x: Answer A: Clinical examination. Peripheral nerve injury: clinical examination is the gold standard.

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman has 9 days of ascending weakness of her legs and arms after a bout of diarrhoea. Reflexes are absent. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 92 bpm, BP 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. A lumbar puncture is performed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on cerebrospinal fluid analysis?
o: Raised protein with a normal white cell count
questions.e: Guillain-Barré syndrome typically shows an isolated rise in CSF protein (albuminocytological dissociation).

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on cerebrospinal fluid analysis?

clues: ascending weakness of her legs and arms
steps.x: Post-infectious ascending areflexic weakness is GBS, whose CSF shows protein without cells.

elim: This suggests bacterial meningitis.
This suggests viral meningitis or encephalitis.
This suggests multiple sclerosis.
This suggests subarachnoid haemorrhage.

steps.x: Answer D: Raised protein with a normal white cell count. GBS CSF: isolated protein rise.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man has 2 years of numbness of his left thumb, index and middle fingers. He has worn a wrist splint and had a steroid injection without lasting benefit, and he now has thenar wasting. He is referred to a hand surgeon, who wants objective evidence of the lesion before operating.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
o: Plain X-ray of the cervical spine
questions.e: Nerve conduction studies confirm and localise median nerve compression at the wrist before decompression surgery.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation?

clues: wants objective evidence of the lesion before operating
steps.x: Before dividing the flexor retinaculum, confirm the lesion electrically.

elim: CT does not assess nerve function.
His symptoms are in a peripheral nerve distribution.
X-ray has little role in confirming a nerve lesion.
This does not confirm carpal tunnel syndrome.

steps.x: Answer C: Nerve conduction studies. Confirm carpal tunnel with nerve conduction studies before surgery.

questions.stem: A 26 year old man woke with a right wrist drop after falling asleep drunk with his arm over the back of a chair. He cannot extend his wrist or fingers, has a small numb patch on the back of the hand at the base of the thumb, and triceps is normal. There is no fracture.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Urgent MRI of the cervical spine
questions.e: Saturday night palsy is treated supportively with a wrist splint and physiotherapy while the nerve recovers.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

clues: falling asleep drunk with his arm over the back of a chair
steps.x: Compression palsy with no fracture: support the wrist and wait for recovery.

elim: IVIG is for Guillain-Barré syndrome, not a focal compression palsy.
Steroids do not speed recovery of a compression palsy.
The history and pattern are classic for Saturday night palsy, not a root lesion.
Compression neurapraxia usually recovers; surgery is not first line.

steps.x: Answer E: Wrist splint and physiotherapy. Radial nerve palsy: wrist splint and physiotherapy.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman has 3 months of tingling in her right thumb, index and middle fingers that wakes her at night. Phalen's test is positive. There is no thenar wasting and thumb abduction is strong. She is not pregnant. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Wrist splint with or without a steroid injection
questions.e: NICE CKS: mild to moderate carpal tunnel syndrome is first treated conservatively with a wrist splint, with or without a steroid injection.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
Mild to moderate carpal tunnel without wasting: conservative first.

elim: Surgery is for symptoms that fail conservative treatment or severe disease.
IVIG is for Guillain-Barré syndrome.
Neuropathic agents are not first line for carpal tunnel syndrome.
This treats ulnar neuropathy at the elbow.

steps.x: Answer E: Wrist splint with or without a steroid injection. Carpal tunnel first line: wrist splint ± steroid injection.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman who is 35 weeks pregnant has 4 weeks of tingling in both thumbs, index and middle fingers, waking her at night. Tinel's test is positive at both wrists. There is no wasting. She asks if she needs an operation. Her BP is 118/72 mmHg and urine dipstick is negative for protein.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Bilateral division of the flexor retinaculum now
Nerve conduction studies before any treatment
Wrist splints; symptoms often settle after delivery
questions.e: Conservative treatment with splints is particularly effective in pregnancy, and the symptoms may settle after delivery.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate advice?

clues: She asks if she needs an operation
steps.x: Pregnancy-related carpal tunnel is common and usually self-limiting.

elim: Surgery is not needed; pregnancy-related carpal tunnel often resolves after delivery.
IVIG is for Guillain-Barré syndrome.
Diagnosis is clinical and splinting can start straight away.
Rest is unnecessary and unhelpful.

steps.x: Answer E: Wrist splints; symptoms often settle after delivery. Carpal tunnel in pregnancy: splint and reassure.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man had a below-knee plaster cast applied for an ankle fracture 2 days ago. He now has tingling over the outer leg and top of his foot and cannot lift his toes. The cast is tight around the upper calf and fibular head. Foot pulses are palpable and capillary refill is 2 seconds.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Ankle-foot orthosis and review in 3 months
Split or adjust the cast to relieve pressure at the fibular head
questions.e: First-line management is treating the cause: remove the compression by adjusting the tight cast.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?

clues: cast is tight around the upper calf and fibular head
steps.x: A tight cast is compressing the common peroneal nerve at the fibular head.

elim: The cause, ongoing compression, must be removed first.
IVIG treats Guillain-Barré syndrome.
This is a focal compression palsy from the cast, not a root lesion.
Neuropathic analgesia does not remove the compression.

steps.x: Answer E: Split or adjust the cast to relieve pressure at the fibular head. Treat the cause: relieve the compression.

questions.stem: A 34 year old chef cut the front of his left wrist deeply with a knife 6 hours ago. He has numbness over the palmar thumb, index and middle fingers and cannot abduct his thumb. The wound is clean. Exploration shows the median nerve completely divided. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Steroid injection into the carpal tunnel
Wrist splint and review in 6 months
questions.e: Complete transection (neurotmesis) has the worst prognosis and needs surgical nerve repair.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management?

clues: cut the front of his left wrist deeply
steps.x: A divided nerve is neurotmesis, which only recovers with surgical repair.

elim: IVIG is for immune neuropathies such as Guillain-Barré.
A transected nerve cannot reconnect without repair.
This treats carpal tunnel syndrome, not a severed nerve.
Delay worsens the outcome of a complete transection.

steps.x: Answer D: Surgical repair of the nerve. Neurotmesis needs surgical repair.

questions.stem: A 24 year old man has a posterior dislocation of his right knee after a motorbike crash. He cannot dorsiflex his right foot and has numbness over the top of the foot. The foot is cool. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 122/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial step?
o: Urgent assessment of the distal pulses and neurovascular status
questions.e: Nerve injury with a fracture or dislocation needs urgent neurovascular assessment; knee dislocation can injure the popliteal artery as well as the common peroneal nerve.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial step?

clues: posterior dislocation of his right knee
steps.x: Common peroneal injury with a cool foot after knee dislocation: check the vessels urgently.

elim: Splinting is for later; limb-threatening injury comes first.
These have no place in the acute trauma setting.
Pain relief for neuropathy does not address a possible vascular injury.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man has 5 days of double vision, unsteady walking and difficulty moving his eyes in all directions, 2 weeks after a diarrhoeal illness. Reflexes are absent and Romberg's test is positive. His forced vital capacity is normal. His pulse rate is 86 bpm and BP 130/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Miller Fisher syndrome (ataxia, areflexia, ophthalmoplegia) is a GBS variant treated with IV immunoglobulin plus supportive care.

Pyridostigmine treats myasthenia gravis.

steps.x: Answer C: Intravenous immunoglobulin. GBS and Miller Fisher: IV immunoglobulin plus supportive care.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman has constant numbness of her right thumb, index and middle fingers and is dropping things. o: Continue the splint for another 6 months
Surgical decompression by division of the flexor retinaculum

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman developed a wrist drop after sleeping with her arm hanging over a chair. Nerve conduction studies show a conduction block across the spiral groove with normal conduction distally. Her function recovers fully within 6 weeks.
questions.q: Which is the most likely grade of nerve injury?
o: Wallerian degeneration of the whole nerve
questions.e: Seddon classification: neurapraxia is a temporary conduction block with the best prognosis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely grade of nerve injury?

steps.x: Answer B: Neurapraxia. Neurapraxia: conduction block, best prognosis.

questions.stem: A 40 year old man had a crush injury to his right forearm. The ulnar nerve is in continuity on exploration but nerve conduction shows no distal response, consistent with axonal degeneration. Over 10 months sensation and power slowly return from proximal to distal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely grade of nerve injury?
questions.e: Axonotmesis: the axon is disrupted but the endoneurium is intact, so the axon can regenerate along it.

steps.x: Axon lost but the sheath intact, guiding slow regeneration.

Absent distal response shows the nerve is damaged.

steps.x: Answer A: Axonotmesis. Axonotmesis: axon disrupted, endoneurium intact, regeneration possible.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has carpal tunnel syndrome. Nerve conduction studies show slowed median nerve conduction across the wrist with normal amplitude responses beyond it. Her symptoms resolve after decompression surgery.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman develops ascending flaccid weakness with absent reflexes 3 weeks after a diarrhoeal illness. Antibodies against peripheral nerve gangliosides are detected. A student asks why an infection of the gut has damaged her nerves.
